hypothesis.hypothesis:
Make the pipeline IF/ID - EX - MEM/WB (4 stages): the MEM stage writes the regfile directly at
the end of its cycle, so the MEM/WB register stops being a pipeline stage.
1. Regfile write port = the MEM-stage merged result (mul | load | add_q | oth_q), rd and
   reg_write from EX/MEM, w_en = EX/MEM.reg_write && valid && !(mem_read && !dmem_ready)
   (a dmem-stalled load does not write; stores never write). The enable decode is early
   (EX/MEM flops plus the ready flop); only the data is late.
2. ID's write-first bypass now captures the instruction two ahead (the one in MEM this cycle)
   instead of the one in MEM/WB. Build ID/EX.rs1_val / rs2_val / b_val as
   `hit ? mem_result : early_value`, where hit (rs == EX/MEM.rd, rd != 0, reg_write) and
   early_value (regfile read, or imm for b_val when alu_src) are formed in parallel, so the late
   MEM result (dmem DO -> align/sext -> OR merge, or DSP -> OR merge) is exactly one LUT from
   the ID/EX flops. Keep the regfile read itself untouched (the bypass is after it, as now).
3. forward_unit keeps only the EX/MEM hit: opsel_t collapses to one bit (rf vs ex), and every
   EX operand copy (rs1 lo/hi/sll/sr/cmp, rs2 lo/hi/cmp, alu_b lo/hi, shamt_l/r) becomes
   `sel ? reg : (add_q | oth_q)`, a single LUT4 per bit. Keep the existing per-copy select-flop
   duplication (now 1 bit per copy) and syn_keep copies.
4. Load-use / MUL-use interlock is unchanged (1 bubble at distance 1); at distance 2 the value
   now arrives through the ID bypass instead of the MEM/WB forward, so CPI is identical
   (cycles must stay at 4,527,646; check with cosim --istall --dstall before synthesis).
5. dmem stall: EX/MEM and ID/EX hold as now. A held ID/EX entry whose operand came from the
   instruction in MEM was bypassed when it was captured, and an instruction captured during
   the stall cycle is discarded by the hold, so no hold_mem_wb retention trick is needed.
   Divider operand latching is unchanged.
6. RVFI retires from the MEM stage: keep a MEM/WB-shaped register (or drive RVFI from EX/MEM
   plus the MEM result with valid = EX/MEM.valid && !dmem_stall) only for RVFI fields; nothing
   in the timed netlist reads it, so synthesis prunes it. rvfi_order increments on that valid.
7. Guard rails for the implementer: do not add any new consumer of take / br_lt_v, do not put
   any logic in front of the regfile read address (it stays the bare imem word), and log the
   cycles/Fmax split plus the top timing paths. If `make timing` shows the DSP -> merge ->
   bypass LUT -> ID/EX path on the wall, fall back for MUL* only: keep a small registered
   MUL result flop and add a MUL distance-2 bubble (lu_arm-style compare against EX/MEM.rd),
   which CoreMark's few MULs can afford; loads keep the one-LUT bypass.
Expected effect: each EX cone loses one LUT/MUX level (~0.4-0.6 ns) and the worst listed
cone (MEM/WB.result -> compare -> PC) disappears as a source; the new late path dmem DO ->
align -> merge -> bypass LUT -> ID/EX is one LUT longer than today's DO -> MEM/WB.result and
must stay under the wall. ~100 MEM/WB flops and the 3:1 mux LUTs go away, which also eases
placement. The stall -> hold -> PC and PC -> PC cones are not shortened, so the gain is capped
by them (~3-6% Fmax at unchanged cycles).

lesson: - 2026-10-01 hyp-20261001-002-r10s1 (regression, -0.20%): Folding WB into MEM made a 4-stage pipeline: MEM writes the flop regfile, ID's write-first bypass captures the MEM-stage merged result one LUT before the ID/EX flops, every one of the twelve EX operand copies shrinks from a 3:1 {rf, wb} mux to a 2:1 `sel ? reg : add_q|oth_q`, and ~100 MEM/WB flops are pruned; it scored 263.95 against r7s0's 264.47, and since fitness = Fmax*1e7/cycles, that is ~119.5 vs 119.7 MHz at the required unchanged 4,527,646 cycles (the split and timing_paths were not logged), far inside r7s0's 5% seed spread, so removing a whole forward source and a LUT/MUX level from every EX cone gained none of the predicted 3-6%; the likely reason is that r7s0's period is set by cones this change did not touch (stall -> hazard -> hold/ID/EX CE and PC -> PC, which r8s0 found level with the forward cone), possibly joined by the new dmem DO/DSP -> merge -> bypass LUT -> ID/EX path, so the EX operand mux is no longer a lever and per-cone LUT savings do not show until every wall cone is cut; yet unlike r8s0 (-4.9%), r9s0 (-12.3%) and r10s0 (-13.8%), which all added copies or chains, this subtractive change held Fmax, so on r7s0 removing logic is Fmax-safe while duplicating it is not, and the leaner 4-stage core is an equally fast base for the next attempt on the stall/PC cones.

title: Re-port r8s2's ahead-indexed offset predictor onto r7s0 with nothing new on br_lt_v/take: train from MEM flops on the used key, no kv/redir/stale bits
motivation:
r8s2 is the best predictor result so far (273.27, +3.33% over r7s0). Its
logged split is 4,245,490 cycles (-6.23% vs r7s0's 4,527,646) at a median
Fmax of 116.0 MHz (seeds 108.3/116.0/116.0), against r7s0's 119.7
(114.3/119.7/119.7). So the CPI gain is measured and real, and the whole
shortfall is a ~3.1% Fmax loss. Its worst path was
EX/MEM.add_q_0 -> u_ex -> u_if/pc_28 (38 cells): the forward ->
br_diff chain -> take -> PC cone that is already on r7s0's wall.
r8s2's lesson names the likely cause. br_lt_v (br_diff[32]) got two new
LUT consumers: take_r_w (which feeds stale_q/redir_q) and the upd_taken
training mux. A take-derived flop (stale_q) was also wired into the
predictor, next to the table and far from EX. Those consumers load the
latest net in the design and pull its placement toward u_bp.
r9s1/r9s2 showed that a registered (2-bubble) redirect is not the fix:
both lost ~13% Fmax in the stall -> kill cone. So keep r8s2's same-cycle
redirect and remove only its extra late consumers.
Break-even: at 4,245,490 cycles the 4.6% bar (276.6) needs
Fmax >= 117.5 MHz, i.e. at most -1.9% vs r7s0. Holding r7s0's 119.7 MHz
gives 282.0 (+6.6%).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Rebuild r8s2's predictor (its RTL is not in git; the plan is in
log.jsonl, id hyp-20261001-003-r8s2) on the current r7s0 RTL. Follow its
rules R1-R4, plus a new rule R5 that r8s2 broke:
  R1 no instruction-word logic and no new LUT/mux level in the PC
     recurrence. The only PC-loop change is the syn_keep'd inc_one
     operand of pc[31:2] + inc_one becoming the flop inc_q.
  R2 no predictor-side flop has take, take_kill, jalr_go, agu_sum or
     br_diff in its D cone.
  R3 take stays the last 2:1 select of pc_d and of the ID/EX kill bits,
     one LUT after br_diff[32].
  R4 nothing new after ID's regfile read or after the ID pc_imm chain.
  R5 (new) br_lt_v / br_diff[32] / br_eq_v drive exactly the same LUTs
     as in r7s0: the six take copies (take_b0..3, take_k0..1) plus the
     RVFI-only branch_cond/branch_trap, which synthesis prunes. Do not
     add a take_r_w, an upd_taken LUT, a stale_q, a redir_q or a kv
     bit. t_lt/t_nlt only change their registered inputs
     (br_inv_t = br_inv ^ p_ok_br).

1. Table (new rtl/fetch_pred.sv), as in r8s2. 64 x {v, ctr[1:0],
   tag[3:0], off[15:2]}, zero-initialized, read address = dedicated
   idx_q with D = if_stage's syn_keep'd pc_alt (no take/jalr_go). The
   read uses LUT-RAM (async read) or the BSRAM mapping r8s2 got; keep
   idx_q's D a bare pc_alt either way. hit = v && ctr[1] && tag match.
   Registered for the next fetch (D-mux holds on `hold`, squashed only
   by the registered ID/EX jump kill bit):
     inc_q = (hit && !jump) ? sext(off) : 30'd1
     pq_q  = hit && !jump;  pq_off_q = off
     pk_q  = {idx_q, ctr}   (the key actually used + ctr snapshot)
   IF keeps a separate kept-constant pc+4 chain for IF/ID.pc4 (link).

2. Verify in ID, exactly as in r8s2: raw-bit B/J offset compare vs
   pq_off -> p_ok_br / p_ok_jal / p_bad. Register br_inv_t, the p_ok
   hi/lo syn_preserve copies (ex_tgt = p_ok ? link : br_target, a flop
   LUT3 ahead of the take mux), jlink, arch_jump (RVFI only), and pk.
   The is_jump kill bit = (dec_is_jump && !p_ok_jal) || p_bad. Keep
   r8s2's formal-proven handling of a p_bad DIV (flush_id jump term
   gated by !ex_busy). Fold that gate into the existing flush LUT so it
   adds no level; ex_busy is register-sourced.

3. Training: all from flops after EX, no new EX consumer. This is what
   changes from r8s2.
   - Key: train at the key the lookup actually used (pk.idx carried
     ID/EX -> EX/MEM). idx_q = pc_alt is a deterministic function of
     the fetch path, so the next lookup on the same path uses the same
     key, and a "wrong" key after a take redirect is self-consistent.
     That is why r8s2's redir_q/stale_q/kv machinery can be dropped.
   - Outcome: recompute the branch condition in MEM from flops:
     EX/MEM.rs1_val / rs2_val (the post-forward operands EX/MEM
     already latches for MUL) and three latched funct3 bits. That is a
     second 33-bit compare + eq on MEM flops into a small upd_* flop
     group (upd_v, upd_taken, upd_key, upd_tag, upd_off, upd_ctr).
     The table write port uses these flops one cycle later (the WB
     cycle), gated by valid && !hold_mem_wb. JAL: taken = 1.
     Update: taken -> {v=1, ctr = hit_snapshot ? sat_inc(ctr) : 2'b10,
     tag, off}; not taken with a hit -> sat_dec(ctr); otherwise no
     write. The 2-cycle-late training costs only a few cold misses.
   - The training offset comes from ID/EX.imm[15:2] latched through
     EX/MEM. Allocate only if imm fits in 14 signed bits and
     imm[1] == 0. This is a register-only condition registered in ID.

4. Before synthesis, measure cycles in cosim (--istall --dstall gives
   the FPGA stall pattern). Expect about 4.24-4.26M, as r8s2 got. If
   it is above 4.30M, fix training before running timing. Then run
   `make timing` and check that no new cell sits between br_diff[32]
   and the PC/kill flops, and that u_bp does not appear in the take
   cone.

Expected: cycles ~4.245M; Fmax 117.5-119.7 MHz (losing back only the
~0.5-1% that the inc_q flop and the extra area cost), so fitness
~277-282 (+5% to +6.6%).

Register br_inv_t, p_ok (syn_preserve hi/lo copies), jlink, arch_jump (RVFI only), the pk key/ctr snapshot, the funct3 bits and an imm-fits/aligned train-enable bit. is_jump kill bit = (dec_is_jump && !p_ok_jal) || p_bad; alu_link stays dec_is_jump. Nothing added after the regfile read or the pc_imm chain.

t_lt/t_nlt use the registered br_inv_t (take stays one LUT after br_diff[32]); no new consumer of br_lt_v/br_eq_v/take (no take_r_w, no upd_taken mux). id_ex_t: br_inv_t, p_ok, jlink, arch_jump, pk (idx/tag/ctr/hit), train_en, off14. ex_mem_t: pk, off14, br funct bits, is-branch/is-jal train flags. No redir/kv/stale fields.

id_ex_jump is now the redefined is_jump kill bit (JALR, unpredicted JAL, p_bad). Gate flush_id's jump term with the register-sourced !ex_busy (as in r8s2) so a p_bad DIV is not killed while iterating; fold it into the existing flush LUT. hold = stall_if && !jump unchanged.

Instantiate fetch_pred. Wire pc_alt/hold/jump into it, inc_q into IF, pq_q/pq_off/pk_q into ID, the MEM-side upd_* flops plus hold_mem_wb into its write port, and jlink/p_ok/link/br_target into the IF muxes.

lesson: - 2026-10-01 hyp-20261001-003-r10s2 (improvement, +5.65%): Re-porting r8s2's ahead-indexed offset predictor onto r7s0 under a rule that br_lt_v/br_diff[32]/br_eq_v drive only r7s0's original take copies (no take_r_w, no upd_taken LUT, no stale_q/redir_q/kv bits; instead training recomputes the branch outcome in MEM with a second 33-bit compare on the EX/MEM rs1_val/rs2_val flops and writes the table in WB at the pk.idx key the lookup actually used, which is self-consistent because idx_q = pc_alt is a deterministic function of the fetch path) scored 279.40, beating r8s2's 273.27 (the best so far), and since fitness = Fmax*1e7/cycles, that is ~118.6 MHz at r8s2's 4,245,490 cycles against r8s2's 116.0 and r7s0's 119.7 (the split was not logged, and the +2.2% over r8s2 lies inside r7s0's 5% seed spread), so removing two LUT loads and one take-derived flop from the latest net in the design seems to have won back about two-thirds of r8s2's ~3.1% Fmax loss while the CPI gain held; so on a flat wall, count every new consumer of a late net as an Fmax cost (not just new LUT levels), and when a later stage needs that net's value, recompute it there from flops, even with a duplicate carry chain, rather than tapping the late net.

title: Fold WB into MEM on the r10s2 predictor core: 2:1 EX operand muxes, no MEM/WB forward leg on the compare->take->PC cone
motivation:
The champion (r10s2, 279.40, 118.794 MHz median, seeds 112.2/118.8/118.8,
4,251,815 cycles) reports its worst path as cpu/u_mem/reg_q.result
(MEM/WB.result) -> u_ex (rs1_cmp/rs2_cmp 3:1 forward mux -> 33-bit br_diff
chain -> take) -> u_if PC, 37 cells / 11 logic levels. MEM/WB.result is
the third leg of every one of the twelve EX operand-mux copies: each bit is
rf ? reg : (wb ? MEM/WB : add_q|oth_q), a 6-input function that Gowin maps
as LUT4 + MUX2_LUT5(+LUT6) instead of one LUT4. r10s1 showed on r7s0 that
removing this leg by folding WB into MEM (regfile written from the
MEM-stage merged result, captured by ID's existing write-first bypass) is
subtractive and Fmax-safe (119.5 vs 119.7 MHz at identical cycles, ~100
fewer flops, -430 LUT4), whereas every additive micro-opt on this base
(r8s0, r9s0, r10s0) lost 5-14%. r10s1 did not gain because r7s0's wall had
other equal cones; r10s2 since then put the predictor's inc_q chain and
verify bits into the design and its single worst listed path now starts
exactly at MEM/WB.result, so the fold attacks the champion's actual top
path while staying in the "remove logic" class that is known to be safe.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Port r10s1's WB-into-MEM fold onto r10s2 without touching the predictor,
the PC mux, the take copies or the hazard/stall cones:
1. mem_stage drives the regfile write port directly from the MEM-stage
   merged result (mul | ld & load_data | add_q | oth_q), gated by
   EX/MEM.ctrl.reg_write && valid && !dmem_stall. The MEM/WB data register
   is no longer a forwarding source; it is kept only as an RVFI-only
   retirement register (pruned from the timed netlist, since nothing timed
   reads it).
2. forward_unit drops the wb leg: the only forward hit is id_ex_rd ==
   if_id_rs (EX/MEM next cycle). A producer two ahead is in MEM while the
   consumer is in ID, so ID's existing write-first bypass (w_en && w_addr
   == rs && rs != 0 ? w_data : rf) already latches its value into ID/EX
   rs?_val / b_val. opsel_t becomes a single bit (rf) per copy; the twelve
   syn_preserve select-flop copies stay, at one bit each.
3. ex_stage: every operand copy (rs1 lo/hi, sll, sr, cmp, rs2 lo/hi/cmp,
   alu_b lo/hi, shamt_l/r) becomes `sel ? reg_val : (add_q | oth_q)`, one
   LUT4 per bit on four flop inputs, so the compare chain, both shifters,
   the adder and the AGU each start one MUX2 level earlier.
4. Load-use / MUL-use interlock unchanged (the 1-bubble still lands the
   load/MUL result in MEM while the consumer is in ID, so the bypass
   catches it). dmem stall: hold_mem_wb disappears; the regfile write is
   simply suppressed while dmem_stall holds EX/MEM, and the frozen ID/EX
   consumer re-captures nothing (ID/EX holds), so the EX/MEM forward source
   stays valid across the stall exactly as today.
5. fetch_pred training stays on the MEM-side upd_* flops (unchanged) and
   the DIV path (early group) is unchanged.
Cycle count must be bit-identical to r10s2 (4,251,815): no interlock or
redirect changes. Fmax: the champion's worst cone loses its MUX2_LUT5
level (~0.3-0.5 ns of 8.42 ns) and ~100 FFs / ~400 LUT4s disappear, which
should loosen placement of the remaining wall cones (stall -> hold -> PC,
PC -> PC). The new path dmem DO -> load align -> merge -> regfile D /
ID bypass -> ID/EX rs?_val (r10s1's option-0 worst, 6 cells) is a short
LUT path; keep it short by leaving the load align one-hot (sel_ld) and
merging into the bypass with the existing compare as the select (no new
level after the 32:1 regfile read: the bypass mux already exists).
Expect +3% (median ~122 MHz); the 4.6% bar is reachable only if the
forward->compare->PC cone was the sole limiter on options 1/2.

lesson: - 2026-10-01 hyp-20261001-001-r11s0 (regression, -3.46%): The same WB-into-MEM fold on r10s2 lost here but won +6.2% as r11s1 in the same round, and the visible difference is the regfile write port: r11s0 wrote the 31x32 flop regfile combinationally from MEM (the late dmem DO -> load align -> merge net, sent in three copies to the ID bypass and the regfile lo/hi halves, with a write enable gated by the bus-ready dmem stall), while r11s1 bypassed the MEM result into ID only as the last AND-OR term (load data last, load align as one-hot lanes registered in EX) and wrote the regfile one cycle later from a registered MEM/WB.{w_en, rd, result} port that is also a second write-first bypass; since fitness = Fmax*1e7/cycles, 269.74 at the required unchanged 4,251,815 cycles means ~114.7 MHz against r10s2's 118.8 (the split and timing_paths were not logged), so removing the MEM/WB leg from the EX muxes paid off only when the late load net and the dmem stall stayed off the 992 regfile flops; so when folding a stage, write bulk storage from a register and let only a bypass mux see the late result, and do not read r10s1's Fmax-neutral direct write on r7s0 as proof that a direct write is safe.

title: 4-stage pipeline on r10s2: fold WB into MEM so MEM/WB.result (r10s2's critical-path source) and hold_mem_wb disappear, every EX operand mux becomes 2:1
motivation:
r10s2 (279.40, 4,251,815 cycles, 118.794 MHz median, seeds
112.2/118.8/118.8) has its worst path starting at
cpu/u_mem/reg_q.result_1 (MEM/WB.result) -> u_ex forward mux -> 33-bit
br_diff chain -> take -> u_if/pc_3 (37 cells, 11 levels). The MEM/WB
forward source is the FIRST cell of that path: every EX operand copy is a
3:1 {rf, wb} mux (LUT4 + MUX2_LUT5) whose wb leg is MEM/WB.result.
r10s1 already showed that folding WB into MEM is Fmax-safe on r7s0
(-0.2%, inside seed noise) while every additive rewrite of the PC/stall
cones lost 5-14% (r8s0, r9s0, r10s0). LESSONS calls the leaner 4-stage
core "an equally fast base for the next attempt on the stall/PC cones".
On r10s2 the fold now removes the exact source of the reported worst
path, and also removes the dmem-stall fanout into MEM/WB (hold_mem_wb
keep-for-forward) and the predictor-update pipeline flop stage, so it
shortens two wall cones (forward -> take -> PC and bus-ready -> stall CE)
at zero CPI cost (CPI is unchanged: MEM already produced the merged
result; the regfile write simply moves one cycle earlier, which is
invisible because the 1-bubble load/MUL interlock still applies).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Make the core IF/ID -> EX -> MEM(+WB) by deleting the MEM/WB register as
a datapath stage, on top of the current r10s2 RTL (keep its predictor
exactly, including the MEM-side recomputed training compare).
0. IMPORTANT (r10s1's logged worst path): r10s1 capped at 119.5 MHz on
   dmem BSRAM DO -> u_mem align/merge -> u_rf/g_reg[*].q (6 cells,
   route-dominated: the late DO-derived w_data net fans out to 31
   regfile words). So do NOT write the flop regfile from the
   combinational MEM result. Instead keep a small registered write port
   w_q = {en, rd, result} (the old MEM/WB.result/rd/reg_write, ~38
   flops) that writes the regfile one cycle after MEM, exactly as today,
   and give id_stage's bypass the MEM-stage result as its LAST 2:1
   select: rs_reg = hit_mem ? mem_result : (hit_wq ? w_q.data : rf_rd),
   with hit_mem / hit_wq from EX/MEM.rd / w_q.rd flops vs the raw rs
   field. The DO-derived net then fans out only to the 3 ID/EX operand
   flops per bit (rs1_val, rs2_val, b_val), never to the regfile, and
   w_q is no longer an EX forward source.
1. mem_stage: the merged result (mul | load | add_q | oth_q) is the
   MEM-stage bypass source (to ID) and the D of w_q.data:
   w_q.en <= EX/MEM.ctrl.reg_write && EX/MEM.valid && !dmem_stall,
   w_q.rd <= EX/MEM.rd. The regfile write port is w_q.
   Keep a register for RVFI only (rvfi fields latched from EX/MEM +
   result + dmem_rdata at the same enable); it has no fabric consumer
   and is pruned from the timed netlist. RVFI order/valid semantics are
   unchanged (retirement = the cycle after MEM completes, as today).
   Remove hold_mem_wb and the "keep data fields for forwarding" logic.
2. Forwarding collapses to two sources. forward_unit computes only the
   EX/MEM hit (id_ex_rd vs if_id rs); the old MEM/WB case is now the
   instruction writing the regfile THIS cycle from MEM, which id_stage's
   existing write-first bypass already merges into ID/EX.rs?_val /
   b_val. opsel_t shrinks to one bit (rf) and every one of the twelve EX
   operand copies (rs1 lo/hi/sll/sr/cmp, rs2 lo/hi/cmp, alu_b lo/hi,
   shamt_l/r) becomes `rf ? reg : (add_q | oth_q)`: one LUT4 per bit,
   no MUX2_LUT5. The branch-compare operand copies feeding br_diff ->
   take -> PC lose one level and the MEM/WB.result source net.
3. Dmem stall: while dmem_ready=0 with a mem op in EX/MEM, the regfile
   write is suppressed (w_en gated) and EX/MEM, ID/EX, PC hold exactly
   as today; the held MEM instruction rewrites on the cycle the bus
   delivers. A load result is then visible to ID via the write-first
   bypass in the same cycle, so the 1-bubble load-use / MUL-use
   interlock is unchanged and sufficient (consumer in ID while the load
   is in MEM gets the bypassed value latched into ID/EX).
   Careful case: a dmem-stalled LOAD in MEM whose consumer is held in
   ID/EX with an rf select captured BEFORE the load wrote. Since the
   interlock kept the consumer out of ID/EX until the load reached MEM,
   the consumer is in ID (not ID/EX) while the load sits in MEM, and ID
   /EX holds on stall_id, so ID re-captures every cycle only when not
   stalled: make the ID/EX data capture enable = !stall_id as today and
   ensure the bypass is sampled on the capturing (non-stalled) cycle,
   i.e. the cycle the load's w_en fires. Also check the divider hold
   (ex_busy) case: the forwarding select for an instruction held in
   ID/EX behind a div must stay valid, which it is because nothing
   ahead of a div writes after the div's operands were latched.
4. Predictor update: upd_* flops are now driven from EX/MEM at the
   MEM-completion cycle (same data, gated by !dmem_stall instead of
   !hold_mem_wb); table write one cycle after MEM, as today.
Expected: CPI identical (4,251,815 cycles; verify in cosim, must match
exactly or within a few cycles). Fmax: the reported worst path loses its
first cell (MEM/WB.result FF) and one MUX2_LUT5 level (~0.3-0.5 ns of
~8.4 ns), and the bus-ready -> stall net loses its MEM/WB (~100-flop)
load. With r10s1's evidence that the fold costs nothing elsewhere, a
+2-5% Fmax gain (121-125 MHz) is plausible; r8s0's lesson warns that
seed spread (~5%) is comparable, so the implementer should run
`make timing` on all placement options and compare against r10s2's
timing_paths on the same option before submitting.

title: Predict JALR (imm=0: returns, indirect calls, switch jumps) through the existing ahead-indexed offset table, verified in EX as a pseudo-BNE on the branch comparator
motivation:
r10s2's ahead-indexed offset predictor (279.40, 4,251,815 cycles, ~118.8 MHz)
predicts only BRANCH / JAL. Every JALR still pays the 1-bubble EX redirect
(is_jump kill bit -> flush_id, jalr_go -> agu_target), and CoreMark at -O3
retires a JALR for every return, every indirect call through a function
pointer (core_list_mergesort's cmp callback -> cmp_idx / cmp_complex) and
every jump-table switch (core_state_transition). Most hot call sites return
to the same caller as last time, and the function pointer / dominant switch
arm repeat, so a "last target" offset predicts most of them. Lessons r6s2,
r8s2, r9s1/r9s2 and r10s2 say a predictor is Fmax-neutral on this base only
if (a) the PC recurrence gains no new mux input or select, (b) nothing new
taps br_lt_v / br_eq_v / take, and (c) training comes from flops after EX.
A JALR target can be expressed as the same pc[31:2] + inc_q offset the table
already applies, so the PC loop is unchanged; and a mispredicted predicted
JALR costs exactly the 1 bubble an unpredicted JALR costs today, so the
prediction is CPI upside only.

Extend r10s2's predictor to JALR with imm[11:0] == 0 (ret, jalr ra,0(aX),
jr aX), with no change to the PC recurrence and no new consumer of the
compare chain:
1. Training (MEM, flops only): for a valid JALR with imm == 0 whose target
   is word-aligned, offset = (EX/MEM.mem_addr - EX/MEM.pc)[15:2] (a MEM-side
   subtract on EX/MEM flops; train only if bits [31:16] are a sign
   extension). Write {v=1, ctr = tm ? sat_inc : 2'b10, tag, off} at the
   pk_idx key the lookup used, exactly like a taken JAL. The table stays
   64 x {v, ctr2, tag4, off14}; the read side, idx_q, inc_q, pq, hold and
   jump squash are unchanged, so IF fetches pc + sext(off) after a
   predicted JALR with no new PC-mux input.
2. Verify (ID, raw bits + flops): p_ok_jalr = pq && valid && dec_is_jalr &&
   instr[31:20] == 0. The predicted target p_tgt = pc + sext({pq_off,2'b00})
   comes from a new ID adder on the pc flop and the pq_off flop (not a tap
   of IF's pc_inc), latched in a new ID/EX field. A verified JALR clears the
   is_jump kill bit (no flush_id, no jalr_go, hold behaves as for a normal
   instruction) and sets the br_ok kill bit, br_use_lt = 0, br_inv_t = 1,
   i.e. it becomes a pseudo "BNE rs1, p_tgt": take = !eq = mispredict, with
   take still one LUT after the compare chain and no new consumer of
   br_lt_v / br_eq_v / take. ctrl.is_branch stays 0 (RVFI / trap unchanged).
3. EX: the rs2_cmp copy's rf source becomes a flop-only LUT
   (pj ? p_tgt : rs2_val), so the late fwd inputs of that mux keep their
   depth; sel_r2_cmp is forced to rf for a verified JALR in ID (as alu_src
   forces sel_b). ex_tgt (the take target) becomes
   sel_lnk ? link : (pj ? agu_target : br_target) with
   sel_lnk = p_ok | (pj & agu_sum[1]) (a misaligned predicted JALR traps to
   link); agu_target thus gains one load per bit, but its path depth

   AGU -> pc_nt -> take mux path. jalr_misalign / the trap clear use
   is_jalr && arch_jump instead of the is_jump kill bit; RVFI pc_next is

noise of 118.8 MHz because the PC loop is untouched and the only new late
loads are one LUT per bit on agu_target. The implementer must first count

lesson: - 2026-10-01 hyp-20261001-003-r11s2 (regression, -2.43%): Extending r10s2's offset predictor to JALR with imm == 0 (trained from MEM flops as mem_addr - pc, and verified in EX as a pseudo "BNE rs1, p_tgt", where p_tgt = pc + sext(pq_off) comes from a new ID adder) followed all three rules that r6s2/r8s2/r10s2 set for an Fmax-neutral predictor (no new PC-mux input or select, no new consumer of br_lt_v/br_eq_v/take, training from flops after EX), yet it scored 272.60; since fitness = Fmax*1e7/cycles, that is at most ~115.9 MHz with no cycle gain and ~112-114.5 MHz at the predicted 4.12-4.20M cycles, against r10s2's 118.8 (the split, the dynamic JALR count and the hit rate that the plan asked for were not logged, and r10s2's own seeds spread 112.2/118.8/118.8, so the no-gain bound alone is within noise); the rules are necessary but not sufficient, because checking a register-target prediction in EX puts rs1 into the compare and the AGU result into the recovery target, and this diff likely paid for both: it ORed p_tgt into the compare copy's rs2 ID/EX value after ID's combinational regfile read (the plan had a flop-only mux in EX, and r6s1/r7s1 found no slack for one more LUT after that read), it made the take-target select depend on agu_sum[1] (forward mux -> AGU carry) instead of the flop p_ok, and it put a `pj ? agu_target : br_target` mux in front of the take mux; so also keep the take-target data and select and the ID regfile-read tail free of new logic, and do not spend a slot on a predictor extension whose expected gain (+3%, low confidence) is below both the 4.6% acceptance bar and the ~5% seed spread unless cosim first shows enough dynamic JALR bubbles to clear that bar.

title: Flatten the MEM->ID bypass: dmem DO and DSP product reach ID/EX operand flops through 2 LUT4s (hit-pre-gated one-hot lanes, split per-consumer sign terms)
motivation:
The champion r11s1 (296.83, 126.2 MHz median, 4,251,815 cycles) has a
logged worst path of only 5 logic cells: dmem BSRAM DO
(dmem_2_dmem_2_0_0_s, byte lane 2, i.e. D[23] = the LB sign bit of lane 2)
-> u_mem load align -> u_id reg_q.rs2_val_12 (a sign-fill bit in [15:8]).
The DO arrives ~2 ns after every fabric flop (r3s0 lesson), and today it
passes through: ld_sign = |(ld_s & {D31,D23,D15,D7}) (8 inputs = 2 LUT
levels, one net fanning out to 24 load bits) -> load_data[15:8] / [31:16]
(another LUT, which then fans out to 4 consumers: rs1_reg, rs2_reg, b_reg
and the w_q result) -> id_stage's `(hit_m ? m_nl : old) | (hit_m & ld)`
LUT -> ID/EX flop. That is 3-4 LUT levels plus two high-fanout routes
after a late hard-block output, which the r3s0/r4s0 lessons say must be
at most one LUT from its consumer. The DSP product (mul_unit sel_lo/sel_hi
AND-OR -> m_nl OR -> bypass LUT) has the same 3-LUT tail after another
late hard block. Every previous round that removed LUT levels after a
late hard-block output at zero CPI paid (r3s0 +36.8%, r4s0 +10%, r11s1
+6.2%), while rounds that added copies/chains on the PC/stall cones lost.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Rebuild the MEM-result bypass into ID/EX (rs1_val, rs2_val, b_val) and the
w_q (MEM/WB.result) D-input as a flat 2-level AND-OR in which every late
bit (dmem DO, DSP product) enters exactly one LUT4 that ANDs it with an
EARLY pre-gated select, followed by one final OR LUT4 into the flop.
Zero CPI change: same pipeline, same interlocks, same values.

1. Pre-gated one-hot selects (early: EX/MEM flops + the ID hit compare on
   the imem word, which is a plain flop in the timed bench). For each ID
   consumer c in {rs1, rs2, b} with hit bit h_c (hit_m1 / hit_m2 /
   hit_mb, computed exactly as today):
     gb_c[k] = h_c & ld_b[k]   (k=0..3, byte lanes for bits [7:0])
     gh0_c   = h_c & ld_h0,  gh2_c = h_c & ld_h2          (bits [15:8])
     gw_c    = h_c & ld_w                                  (bits [31:16])
     gs_c[k] = h_c & ld_s[k] (ld_s already folds sext/width; split into
               two copies: one ANDed with ld_hx for [15:8], one with ld_wx
               for [31:16], so the fill needs no extra AND after DO)
     gml_c   = h_c & sel_mlo, gmh_c = h_c & sel_mhi        (DSP halves)
   For w_q the same selects without h_c (the existing EX/MEM ld_* /
   sel_m* flops).
2. Sign fill as two pre-gated half-terms per consumer, each a single LUT4
   straight off DO: SX = gs[0]&D[7] | gs[1]&D[15], SY = gs[2]&D[23] |
   gs[3]&D[31]. Keep one (syn_keep) SX/SY pair per consumer and per
   upper group ([15:8] and [31:16]), so no DO-derived net drives more
   than ~16 loads (today ld_sign drives 24 bits, each of which fans to 4
   consumers).
3. Per-bit final OR LUT4 (syn_keep on the level-1 terms so synthesis
   cannot re-chain them):
     [7:0]  : base | L01 | L23,   L01 = gb[0]&D[i] | gb[1]&D[i+8],
                                   L23 = gb[2]&D[i+16] | gb[3]&D[i+24]
     [15:8] : base | Lh | SX | SY, Lh = gh0&D[i] | gh2&D[i+16]
     [31:16]: base | (gw&D[i]) | SX | SY  (gw&D[i] folded into the final
              LUT with base when it fits, else its own LUT)
   with the DSP term LM = gml&P[i] | gmh&P[i+32] (one LUT4 off the DSP
   output) folded into base's side, never behind a DO term.
   base = hit ? (add_q | oth_q) : old  (old = hit_w ? w_data : rf_read,
   unchanged), i.e. the regfile-read side keeps today's LUT count and the
   ALU halves come straight from EX/MEM flops; mul_result is no longer
   inside m_nl for the bypass.
4. mem_stage exports the raw DO word, the DSP product halves and the
   EX/MEM select flops to id_stage instead of the pre-merged load_data /
   nl_result; w_q.result uses the same 2-level structure (its own select
   and sign-term copies). mul_unit keeps both ALTOPS and real branches;
   under ALTOPS the stand-in output is simply treated as the gated
   product (lo term, hi term 0) so formal still covers the bypass.

Why it should help: the worst path drops from 5 cells (3-4 LUTs + two
fanout-24/fanout-4 routes after a ~2 ns-late BSRAM DO) to 2 LUTs with
fanout <=16, worth roughly 1-1.5 ns on that cone; the DSP->bypass cone
loses one LUT the same way. At 7.92 ns that would move the limit to the
next tier (ALU forward loop / take -> PC / AGU -> dmem ADB), which r11s1
did not touch and which earlier rounds measured at roughly 0.4-0.8 ns
below this one, so expect ~+4-7% Fmax at identical cycles. The change is
subtractive on the late nets and only adds early (flop-sourced) select
LUTs (~40-60 LUT4), never a new consumer of br_lt_v / take / the stall
nets and no new PC-mux input, respecting the r8s0-r10s0 and r10s2 rules.
The implementer should run `make timing` on all three placement options
and record the top paths and the cycles/Fmax split.

Measured on the champion (make timing, placement option 0, 115.3 MHz):
the top 5 paths are a flat wall within 0.02 ns, and 3 of the 4 distinct
cones end at the SAME ID/EX operand flops:
  13.968 ns  5 cells  dmem DO (lane 2) -> u_mem -> u_id rs2_val_12
  13.963 ns 35 cells  EX/MEM.oth_q fwd -> branch compare -> take_kill -> kill_q
  13.954 ns  4 cells  imem lfsr -> u_rf 32:1 read -> u_id rs2_val_5
  13.951 ns  5 cells  DSP prod -> u_mul -> u_id rs2_val_19
So the restructure MUST also flatten the regfile-read side, or it only
moves the wall by 0.02 ns: pre-gate sel_rf = !hit_m & !hit_w (early,
imem-flop compares) and fold all flop-sourced alternatives into one
early term E = (hit_w & !hit_m & w_data) | (hit_m & (add_q|oth_q)),
so the 32:1 read-mux output enters only the final OR LUT
((sel_rf & rf) | E | late terms; use a LUT5 = 2 LUT4 + MUX2_LUT5 where
the input count exceeds 4, never a third LUT level). Do not touch the
take -> kill cone (r9s0 showed chain-splitting it loses); this round
targets the other three cones, all of which share the ID/EX operand
capture tail.

lesson: - 2026-10-01 hyp-20261001-001-r12s0 (regression, -17.44%): Rebuilding r11s1's MEM->ID bypass as flat per-consumer AND-OR terms (the raw dmem DO word and both raw 32-bit DSP product halves exported to ID; every byte/half/word lane, sign half-term and mul-half select pre-ANDed with each consumer's hit for rs1/rs2/b, plus a w_q copy; syn_keep'd 32-bit e1/e2/eb early terms) scored 245.06, which at the required unchanged 4,251,815 cycles means ~104.2 MHz (7.92 -> ~9.60 ns, +1.7 ns, below even the champion's placement-option-0 115.3 MHz, so not placement noise; the split and the three-option timing_paths that the plan asked for were not logged); the likely cause is that it bought "two LUTs after the late output" by copying the first LUT once per consumer, so by the plan's structure each DO bit went from ~4 LUT loads (one shared byte/half/word/sign align) to ~20 and each of the 64 raw DSP bits from 1 load to 4, and that its "early" selects were not early, because the hit compare runs on the imem word, which already starts the champion's 4-cell imem -> 32:1 regfile read -> rs2_val wall cone, and pre-gating put that compare plus a new AND level in series in front of the DO AND, where r11s1 had hit_m enter the final LUT directly; so for a late hard-block output, do the first merge once next to the block and copy only its output (as r4s0/r6s0 did), count fanout added on the block's output pins as a cost (as r10s2 did for br_lt_v), and treat any select derived from the ID instruction word as already on the wall, not as an early flop.

title: LUT-RAM register file: replace the 992-flop / 31-control-set regfile and its two 32:1 flop read-mux trees with two async-read distributed-RAM copies written from w_q, shrinking the die-spread, route-dominated timing wall
motivation:
A local `make timing TARGET=bench` on the champion (r11s1, place option 0,
115.3 MHz; options 1/2 at 126.2) shows the flat-wall pattern again: at
least nine different cones end within 0.17 ns of each other (-3.674 ..
-3.50 ns slack):
  1. dmem BSRAM DO -> load align (3 LUTs) -> ID bypass -> ID/EX.rs2_val   (5 cells)
  2. EX/MEM.oth_q -> EX fwd mux -> branch compare -> take -> ID kill_q    (35 cells)
  3. lfsr_24 (= io_imemData bit 24, rs2[4]) -> u_rf 32:1 read mux select
     -> ID bypass -> ID/EX.rs2_val                                        (4 cells)
  4. MUL DSP prod -> MEM merge -> ID bypass -> ID/EX.rs2_val              (5 cells)
  5. ID/EX.rs1_val -> divider quo_q; 6. oth_q -> IF pc; 7. rs1_val ->
     shifter -> oth_q; 8. lfsr -> ID pc+imm -> br_target; 9. dmem_ready -> pc
These paths are dominated by routing, not by logic. Path 3 has 7.17 ns of
route out of an 8.6 ns data delay (83%): one 4.06 ns net from the
instruction-word flop (fanout 40) to the regfile mux at R12C44, then
1.1 + 0.4 + 1.6 ns more back to the ID/EX flop at R21C16. Path 1 has
4.75 ns of route out of 8.6 ns. The 31x32 flop regfile is the largest
structure in the design: 992 of the 1896 FFs, ~550 LUT/MUX cells for the
two 32:1 read trees, and 31 distinct clock-enable control sets
(w_en && w_addr == i). On GW2A the two FFs of a CLS share CE/SR
(r10s0 lesson), so those 31 control sets pack loosely, and every other
cone in the wall has to route around this block.
The last two winners were subtractive (r10s1, Fmax-neutral; r11s1, +6.2%).
The three rounds that added copies or chains (r8s0, r9s0, r10s0) all lost.
This hypothesis is subtractive too: it removes ~1000 FFs and ~300 LUTs,
adds no CPI cost, and leaves no wall cone with more logic levels.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Change the register file from flip-flops to Gowin distributed RAM (SSRAM,
RAM16SDP4 cells with asynchronous read and synchronous write). Keep the
pipeline, bypasses and timing boundaries exactly as they are:
  - Two copies of a 32x32 array, one per read port (rs1, rs2), each tagged
    /* synthesis syn_ramstyle = "distributed_ram" */. Both copies are
    written by the single registered write port that already exists,
    w_q = MEM/WB.{w_en, rd, result}. Every write-port input is a flop, so
    no late net (dmem DO, DSP output, dmem_ready) reaches the RAM, as the
    r11s0/r11s1 lessons require.
  - The reads stay combinational in ID and are addressed by the raw
    instruction-word bits, as now. A 32-deep SDP read is 2 x 16-deep
    banks plus one 2:1 select on rs[4]. Its depth is about the same as
    the current LUT4 + MUX2_LUT5..F8 tree, but each port now spans 16
    RAM16SDP4 cells (~8 CLUs per bank) instead of 32 x 32:1 trees spread
    over ~500 cells, so the long nets from the instruction word to the
    read mux and from the read mux to the ID bypass get much shorter.
  - A same-cycle read-during-write returns the old contents, exactly
    like the flop array. The existing write-first bypass
    (hit_w ? w_data : rf_rd) in id_stage already covers it, so the
    semantics are unchanged.
  - x0: entry 0 of the RAM is never written (the RAM write enable is
    w_en && w_addr != 0, all flops) and is zero-filled by an `initial`
    loop. ID must not rely on
    that, because LUT-RAM INIT handling differs between Gowin, Verilator
    and Yosys. Fold an `rs_addr == 0` force-to-zero into the existing
    write-first bypass LUT instead:
    rs_old = z ? 0 : (hit_w ? w_data : rs_data). That is still one LUT4
    per bit (z, hit_w, w_data, rs_data). z is computed from the
    instruction word in parallel with the RAM read, so the ID tail gains
    no level (r6s1/r7s1: no slack for one more LUT after the regfile
    read).

CE control sets, and a much smaller die footprint. Path 3 should lose
1-3 ns of route. The other wall cones (DO -> ID bypass, compare -> take ->
PC/kill, DSP -> ID, shifter, divider) should each gain a few hundred ps
from shorter routes on a denser placement. CPI is unchanged by
construction (cycles must stay at 4,251,815), so every MHz is fitness.
Target: a median Fmax of ~132-136 MHz (+5-8%), with the worst seed lifted
from 115 MHz.
Failure mode to watch: if Gowin maps the array back to flops (the
attribute is ignored) or to BSRAM (a synchronous read adds a cycle and
breaks the design), check the synthesis report for the SSRAM/RAM16SDP4
count (the eval logs `lutram`). Try syn_ramstyle "distributed_ram" first,
then "select_ram", and as a last resort instantiate RAM16SDP4 primitives
explicitly under an `ifdef` that only the Gowin flow sees, keeping the
behavioral array for Verilator/Yosys. Keep the result only if lutram > 0
and the flop count drops by ~900+.

title: Load-address predictor: ahead-indexed last-address+stride table lets a predicted load read dmem in its EX cycle, removing the load-use bubble
motivation:
Measured in cosim on the r11s1 champion (this hypgen run, CoreMark
ELF, retire-gap attribution with no bus stalls, whole program):
  branch not-taken bubbles   22.9K   (236K BRANCH not taken)
  branch taken bubbles       26.1K   (296K BRANCH taken)
  JAL bubbles                 5.8K   (49.6K JAL)
  JALR bubbles               13.8K   (13.8K JALR)
  LOAD-use bubbles          207.7K   (547K loads)
  MUL-use bubbles            35.7K   (94K MUL)
Growing fetch_pred from 64 to 512 entries (same BSRAM, measured with
--istall --dstall) cut bench cycles only 4,251,815 -> 4,241,240
(-0.25%), and r11s2's JALR prediction saved ~10K. All remaining
control-flow bubbles together are ~69K (~1.6% of 4.24M), so no
branch/JAL/JALR predictor can clear the 4.6% acceptance bar. The
only predictable bubble source big enough is the load-use interlock:
~208K bubbles, ~4.9% of bench cycles (CoreMark list traversal
ptr->next->info chains, state-machine byte loads, matrix loads).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Predict load addresses one stage early so a predicted load reads the
dmem BSRAM during its EX cycle instead of MEM:
1. New rtl/ld_pred.sv: an ahead-indexed table (same key as fetch_pred:
   the fetch-address flop idx_q path, 64-256 entries, LUT-RAM or BSRAM
   with registered read) holding {v, conf[1:0], last_addr[19:2],
   stride[7:2]} per load PC. Read in IF, its prediction (pred_addr =
   last + stride, formed into a flop before the load reaches ID) is a
   register by the time the load is in ID.
2. When the instruction in ID is a confident predicted LOAD and the
   instruction in EX is NOT a memory op (dmem port free next cycle),
   the dmem address register D takes pred_addr (a flop-only 2:1 mux
   in front of the absorbed EX/MEM.mem_addr BSRAM address register,
   select from flops). The DO then arrives during the load's EX
   cycle; EX latches DO through the existing one-hot load-lane
   AND-OR into a new EX/MEM load-result field, and verifies
   pred_addr == agu_sum into a flop (ends at a flop, no new consumer
   of take / br_lt_v).
3. The hazard_unit's load-use interlock is skipped for a predicted
   load (registered bit, decided in ID from flops), so the consumer
   enters EX one cycle behind it and picks the loaded value from the
   EX/MEM forward source (load result ORed into the existing
   add_q|oth_q path, which is 0 for loads today).
4. Misprediction (verify flop = 0) or a dmem stall on the early read:
   the load re-executes normally in MEM and the already-issued
   consumer is squashed and refetched via the existing p_bad-style
   "jump to link" redirect of the load (1-2 bubble penalty, rarer than
   the bubble saved). Training from MEM flops (actual mem_addr) like
   fetch_pred.
Implementer MUST first prototype the cycle effect in cosim with
--istall --dstall and only proceed to synthesis if bench cycles fall
by >= 4% from 4,251,815; report the predicted-load coverage, the
port-conflict rate and the mispredict count. Keep every new select a
flop, keep DO at most one LUT from its new EX/MEM flop, and add
nothing to the stall -> hold/kill cone except registered bits
(r9s1/r9s2 lesson).

lesson: - 2026-10-01 hyp-20261001-003-r12s2 (regression, +0.00%): A last-address+stride load-address predictor (ld_pred.sv, early dmem read in EX, consumer squashed through a jump to mlink on a mispredict) was dropped at its own cosim gate and nothing shipped, because most of CoreMark's ~208K load-use bubbles come from pointer chasing (ptr->next) and data-dependent addresses that last+stride cannot predict: only 28.7% of loads got a confident prediction, 24% of those lost the dmem port to a memory op just ahead, and 43.0K of 114.4K early reads failed (25.1K only because the dmem bus was not ready), so cycles moved -0.27% with --istall --dstall and +0.19% without stalls, far below the 4% bar even before any Fmax cost; address prediction will not remove load-use bubbles on this benchmark, and the cheap cosim gate (coverage, port-conflict and mispredict counters before synthesis) is worth requiring for any speculative-CPI idea.

title: Fill the predictor's BSRAM: grow fetch_pred from 64 to 512 direct-mapped entries (same block, same tag width, same logic depth)
motivation:
fetch_pred's table is 64 x 21 bits behind a registered index (idx_q), so
Gowin maps it to one BSRAM (lutram = 0 and only 1896 FFs in the
champion), which holds 512 x 36 in SDPX9B mode. 87% of the block is unused.
With 64 sets indexed by pc[7:2], every hot B/J site whose key address
matches another one mod 256 bytes evicts it. CoreMark's hot loop spans the
list, matrix, state and crc kernels, about 4-6 KB of text, so 64 direct-mapped
sets thrash. Each conflict miss costs a taken-branch bubble, and a
tag-aliased hit costs a p_bad bubble plus an invalidate. The predictor already
cut 282K of 4.53M cycles (r7s0 -> r8s2), and the leftover miss traffic is
the cheapest CPI left to recover: the cycle count is deterministic, unlike
the ~5% placement noise that has sunk every recent Fmax-only micro-opt.

title: Decoupled fetch: 4-entry instruction queue with a flop head as ID's word; PC hold from flops only
motivation:
Champion r11s1: 4,251,815 cycles for ~2.94M retired instructions. The imem
port delivers at most one word per cycle with ~21.9% not-ready cycles
(xorshift accept 100/128), so the fetch bound is 2.94M / 0.781 = ~3.76M
cycles. About 0.49M cycles sit above that bound. Most of them are imem-ready
cycles thrown away while the back end is stalled: the PC holds on dmem freezes
(~0.25M stall cycles), load-use/MUL-use bubbles (~208K, measured in r12s2) and
divider iterations, so a ready fetch in those cycles is lost. Then every later
imem stall still costs a full bubble.
Timing (`make timing`, option 0, this checkout): the top 25 paths form a flat
wall within 0.22 ns. It covers dmem DO / DSP -> ID bypass -> rs2_val,
lfsr(imem) -> 32:1 regfile -> rs2_val, EX/MEM.oth_q fwd -> compare -> take ->
kill_q RESET and PC, rs1_val -> divider negate, the shifter -> oth_q,
lfsr -> imm -> pc+imm -> br_target, and stall_gen/dmem_ready -> PC. So no
single-cone Fmax cut can clear the 4.6% bar (r12s1 lesson). The lever left is
cycles, at no new logic on any of those cones.
Earlier fetch-queue attempts lost on Fmax because the queue/skid head was a mux
in front of the regfile read (r6s1), or because they added a take consumer
(r8s1). This design avoids both.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Insert an instruction queue (IQ) between the imem and ID. Its head is always a
plain flop, so ID's word is still a bare register, as the LFSR imem word is
today. That keeps r6s1's rule: no mux in front of the regfile read, decoder,
imm_gen or load-use compare.
- IQ: 4 entries {instr, pc, pc4, pk_* predictor snapshot, valid}, with a
  registered count. The head register's D is a 3:1 from flops:
  hold / entry[1] / imem word. The select is pop && count/valid state, and
  pop = ID/EX captures a valid head (= !stall_id && !flush).
- Fetch: the PC advances when imem_ready && !full_q, where full_q is a
  registered, conservative "count >= 3". So hold = !imem_ready || full_q
  (or the divider-busy/jump terms as needed, from flops). That takes
  dmem_ready, the load-use compare and ex_busy out of the PC recurrence
  (wall path 15, dmem_ready -> pc_9). The predictor (pc + inc_q,
  idx_q <= pc_alt) is unchanged and is pushed into the IQ beside the word.
  Its key is still a deterministic function of the fetch path.
- Redirect: take / jalr_go / jump still steer the PC exactly as now (no new
  take consumer, no new PC-mux level). The IQ is flushed one cycle later by a
  registered flush_q, built from the same registered ID/EX jump bit plus a
  single fanout-1 take-derived flop. flush_q kills the wrong-path head at
  ID/EX capture (a flop-sourced kill term) and clears the IQ valids/count.
  The redirect target's imem word arriving in that cycle is written into the
  empty head.
  A mispredict/JALR then costs 2 bubbles instead of 1. r9s1 measured exactly
  this doubling on the predictor core: +53K cycles (4,245,490 -> 4,298,818).
- Back-end stalls (dmem freeze, load-use, MUL-use, divider) no longer stop
  fetch. Up to 3-4 ready fetches are banked and later cover imem stalls.
  r6s1's 2-entry fall-through queue saved 158K cycles without a predictor.
  Here the queue is deeper and redirects that flush it are fewer, so
  ~180-230K is saved, minus 53K for the extra redirect bubble, for a net of
  ~-3 to -4% cycles.
Cosim gate (r8s1/r12s2 lessons): before synthesis, run coremark cosim with
--istall --dstall and log cycles, IQ-full cycles, flush count and banked
fetches. Proceed only if cycles are <= 4.10M (>= 3.6% cut).
Fmax: no added logic on any of the wall cones. The PC-hold cone gets shorter.
New logic (head D-mux, pop/count) sits on flop-sourced selects except pop,
which carries the same stall_id fanout that the ID/EX CE carries today.
The IQ adds ~4x~100 FFs.

changes.description: New module: 4-entry IQ (instr, pc, pc4, pk snapshot, valid). Flop head register with a 3:1 D-mux (hold / entry[1] / imem), registered count and full_q, push on imem_ready && !full_q, pop on ID capture, clear on registered flush_q.
hold = !imem_ready || full_q (plus flop-only jump/busy terms); keep the take / jalr_go / jump PC-mux order unchanged; export the fetched {pc, pc4, word} to the IQ instead of straight to ID.

Instantiate fetch_queue between u_if and u_id; route the IQ head (always a flop) as if_id_w; hazard/forward units read the head's rs fields; build flush_q from a fanout-1 take-derived flop and the registered jump kill bit.

lesson: - 2026-10-01 hyp-20261001-002-r13s1 (regression, -7.31%): A 4-entry decoupled instruction queue that kept r6s1's rule (the IQ head is a plain flop and is ID's word, so no mux sits in front of the regfile read or decoder), held the PC only on imem_ready and a registered full_q, and flushed one cycle late from a registered take_q|jq_q scored 275.13; since fitness = Fmax*1e7/cycles, that is ~117.0 MHz at the unchanged 4,251,815 cycles and <= ~112.8 MHz if the planned <= 4.10M cosim gate was met, against r11s1's 126.2, and holding 126.2 MHz would have taken ~4.59M cycles (+7.9%) (the split and the gate counters were not logged); the likely cause is that decoupling fetch moves the back-end stall cone instead of removing it: pop (ID/EX captures the head, i.e. !stall_id) still carries dmem_ready and the load-use compare on the ID word, and it now selects the ~94-bit head D-mux (instr, pc, pq/pk_* snapshot) plus the count and entry updates instead of the PC hold, while the "registered" flush still needed a new syn_keep take copy (take_f_w -> take_q) on the compare -> take wall cone that r8s1 had flagged; with r6s1 (mux head, -4.03%), r8s1 (skid, -1.85%) and this flop-head IQ (-7.31%) all losing, assume the stall net must reach whatever register sits at the fetch/ID boundary, and do not build another fetch buffer unless cosim first shows a cycle cut clearly above both the 4.6% bar and these 2-7% losses.

title: Predictor-steered fetch-ahead: keep fetching down fetch_pred's predicted path while ID is held, so banked instructions hide later imem stalls
motivation:
Branch prediction is already used up as a CPI lever on r11s1. r12s2's cosim
attribution on the champion found that all control-flow bubbles together
(not-taken 22.9K, taken 26.1K, JAL 5.8K, JALR 13.8K) come to about 69K,
roughly 1.6% of 4,251,815 cycles. Growing fetch_pred from 64 to 512
entries saved only 0.25%, and r11s2's JALR prediction saved about 10K
cycles. So a better direction or target predictor cannot clear the 4.6%
bar.
The largest remaining cost is the imem bus stall. About 22% of cycles have
io_imemReady = 0, and each one costs a full bubble whenever the backend
could have moved forward. That is on the order of 0.9M cycles, against
about 0.3M for load-use plus MUL-use bubbles. The core cannot overlap any
of it today, because the PC holds and the fetched word is thrown away
whenever ID is held: about 208K load-use, 36K MUL-use and roughly 150K
dmem-stall hold cycles, plus divider holds.
fetch_pred already turns the PC sequence into a predicted fetch path. Its
inc_q advance is a flop, and idx_q is a deterministic function of the
fetch path. That means the front end can run ahead of a held ID down the
predicted path, the same idea as a decoupled branch-predictor/fetch-target
queue. Each word banked during a hold cycle later hides one imem stall.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Let IF keep fetching down fetch_pred's predicted path while ID is held.
Bank up to two fetched words in a small queue, and have ID use a banked
word in any cycle where it would otherwise get an imem-stall bubble.
STEP 0 is a mandatory cosim gate, before any synthesis. Add the queue
behaviour to the RTL and run CoreMark cosim with --istall --dstall, which
reproduces the FPGA stall pattern cycle for cycle. Log three things: bench
cycles, the number of imem-stall cycles hidden, and the number of banked
words flushed by redirects. Ship only if bench cycles drop at least 6%
below 4,251,815, i.e. to about 3.99M or fewer. Otherwise stop and report
the counters, as r12s2 did.
Hand estimate: about 312K hold cycles have imem ready (400K x 0.78), so
about that many words can be banked. A flush happens only on an
unpredicted redirect, about 69K events, and loses at most 2 words each.
With a 22% stall rate, a banked word is almost always used before the
next flush, which is about 40 instructions away. That gives roughly
180-260K hidden stall cycles, a 4-6% cut. The gate tells us whether the
real number reaches that.
Mechanism. The rules come from the earlier fetch-queue lessons: r6s1
-4.0% and r8s1 -1.85%, plus the r10s2 rule about loading late nets.
1. Queue: q0/q1 hold {instr, pc, pc4, pred snapshot pq/pq_off/pk_*}.
   q0 is captured on the first hold cycle; this is the word ID is
   holding. Words fetched during later hold cycles, with imem ready,
   are appended. The PC advances down pc + inc_q (the predicted path)
   while the queue is not full. pc_alt becomes
   (hold && q_full_q) ? pc : pc_reg, where q_full_q is a flop. This
   replaces the hold select inside the same LUT, with no new level.
   fetch_pred's hold input becomes the same qualified hold, so its
   prediction flops advance together with the PC.
2. Feeding ID without adding a LUT level in front of the regfile read.
   r6s1 lost 4% because it put a 2:1 mux on the regfile read address.
   Instead, as r8s1 did, the queue head gets its own second 32:1
   regfile read, decoder and forward/load-use compare, all running from
   q0 flops, which are early. The registered select use_q_q picks
   between the two finished ID results only in the existing last
   bypass LUT before the ID/EX flops (hit_m/m_ld_data stay the final
   AND-OR terms). The imem-word path is unchanged.
3. Flushing on a redirect. Queued words are on the predicted path, so
   they are wrong exactly when EX redirects: take (a mispredict) or
   jump. The cycle after that, ID must decode the redirected imem
   word and not q0, so the queue-valid and use_q_q flops must drop in
   the same cycle. The jump term is a flop (ID/EX is_jump). take is
   the latest net in the design. r8s1 likely lost Fmax by sending a
   take copy into IF, and r10s2 showed that every consumer of
   br_lt_v counts. So take gets exactly one new consumer: a single
   syn_keep'd LUT `qkill = lt ? t_lt : t_nlt` that feeds only the
   D-inputs of the three flops q0_v, q1_v and use_q_q, as the last
   AND (not CE or SR), placed next to them. Nothing else in the queue
   sees take, br_lt_v or br_eq_v. Fallback if timing shows this LUT
   on the worst path: register take into one flop, and on the next
   cycle kill the ID/EX capture (inside kill_nt's existing
   reset/flush LUT) and hold the PC. That costs one bubble per
   redirect while the queue is non-empty; count it in the gate.
   A word that leaves the queue into ID during the redirect cycle
   itself is already removed by take_kill / flush_id, like today's
   wrong-path imem word.
4. imem-stall use: when q0 is valid and the backend can advance, ID
   takes q0 whatever io_imemReady is. The IF word fetched that cycle is
   appended if it is valid. flush_if (valid = 0) applies only when
   the queue is empty.
Expected outcome: a 4-6% cycle cut, if the gate confirms it, at an Fmax
cost held to about 1-2%, because the PC recurrence, take, and the
imem-to-regfile path are untouched. The net is about +3%, with low
confidence; this is the only predictor-steered angle whose CPI headroom
is above the bar.

lesson: - 2026-10-01 hyp-20261001-003-r13s2 (regression, +0.00%): Predictor-steered fetch-ahead (IF keeps fetching down fetch_pred's path while ID is held, banking up to 2 words that ID uses on imem-stall cycles) stopped at its own cosim gate with nothing shipped: with --istall --dstall it cut 4,251,815 -> 4,007,317 cycles (-5.75%, 195,378 imem stalls hidden, 19,279 words flushed, 121,936 refused when full), 10.6K short of the 6% gate, and a 4-deep queue reached only -6.05% (+12.6K), because a 1-word/cycle front end can bank words only during backend holds and 578,140 imem bubbles still arrive with the queue empty; so ~6% is the ceiling for hiding imem stalls behind holds, which the 1.85-7.31% Fmax losses of r6s1/r8s1/r13s1 would mostly cancel, and queue depth is not the limit, so a further attack on imem stalls needs fetch bandwidth above 1 word/cycle (or fewer stalls), not a deeper or cleverer queue.

title: Three subtractive wall-cone cuts: flop-preANDed load sign fill, divider prep cycle, B/J/U-only imm for the ID pc+imm adder
motivation:
The champion r11s1 (296.83; 115.3/126.2/126.2 MHz; 4,251,815 cycles) logs
the same worst path on every no-RTL-change rerun (r12s2, r13s0, r13s2):
dmem BSRAM DO (dmem_2_..., lane 2 = D[23], an LB sign bit) -> u_mem ->
u_id reg_q.rs2_val_12 (a sign-fill bit of [15:8]), 5 cells. Today a
sign-fill bit is the deepest load bit: ld_sign = |(ld_s & {D31,D23,D15,D7})
is an 8-input AND-OR (2 LUT levels) whose output fans out to 24 bits,
then it is ANDed with ld_hx / ld_wx and ORed with the lane pair (3rd LUT),
then id_stage's bypass LUT (4th). The byte lanes [7:0] are only 3 LUTs
deep (two pair LUTs, OR, bypass). So the logged worst path is one LUT and
one fanout-24 route longer than the other load bits, purely because of
how the sign is formed, and the fix needs no new consumer of DO.
r12s1's local option-0 path list showed a flat wall of ~9 cones within
0.17 ns. Two other cones on that list have equally cheap, purely
subtractive cuts:
  (5) ID/EX.rs1_val -> EX forward mux -> divider a_mag/b_mag negate
      (a 32-bit carry chain) -> quo_q / dvs_q at div start;
  (8) imem word (bench lfsr flop) -> imm_gen (7-bit opcode case, 2 LUT
      levels) -> pc + imm carry chain -> ID/EX.br_target.
Lessons that constrain the design: r12s0 (-17%) lost by copying the first
DO merge per consumer and pre-gating it with the ID hit compare, so here
the first merge stays once in MEM, hit stays in the final LUT, and no DO
pin gains a load. r8s0/r9s0/r10s0 lost by adding copies or chains to the
PC/stall cones, while the subtractive r10s1/r11s1 held or raised Fmax, so
every change below removes logic from a cone and touches no PC, stall,
take or kill net. CPI is unchanged except +1 cycle per DIV/REM (the
CoreMark timed loop has almost no divides, per r1s0).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Three independent zero-CPI changes, each removing at least one LUT
level (or a carry chain) from a cone on the champion's wall:

1. Load sign fill from pre-ANDed flops (cone 1, the logged worst path).
   In EX, register per-lane, per-group fill selects instead of one ld_s:
     sf_h[k] = ld && sext && byte-load && lane==k         (fill for [15:8])
     sf_w[k] = ld && sext && !word && (sign lane == k)   (fill for [31:16])
   (sf_h is ld_s & {4{ld_hx}}; sf_w is ld_s & {4{ld_wx}}; both are just
   the existing ld_s D-logic ANDed with the existing ld_hx / ld_wx
   D-terms, so they are EX-side flop inputs, not new DO logic). In MEM:
     X01 = sf_h[0]&D7 | sf_h[1]&D15,  X23 = sf_h[2]&D23 | sf_h[3]&D31
     Y01 = sf_w[0]&D7 | sf_w[1]&D15,  Y23 = sf_w[2]&D23 | sf_w[3]&D31
     load_data[15:8][i]  = (ld_h0&D[8+i] | ld_h2&D[24+i]) | X01 | X23
     load_data[31:16][i] = ld_w&D[16+i] | Y01 | Y23
   so every load bit is 2 LUTs after DO (pair/fill LUT4s, then one OR
   LUT4) and 3 with ID's unchanged bypass LUT, the same depth as the
   [7:0] byte lanes today. The X nets fan out to 8 bits and the Y nets to 16,
   instead of one ld_sign net to 24; D7/D15/D23/D31 each drive 2 fill
   LUTs instead of 1 ld_sign LUT (+1 load on 4 DO pins, versus r12s0's
   ~16 extra per pin). Keep `syn_keep` on X01/X23/Y01/Y23 so synthesis
   does not re-form a shared ld_sign. load_data stays a single exported
   net per bit (ld_data port), id_stage's `(hit_m ? m_nl : old) |
   (hit_m & m_ld_data)` final LUT and the w_q merge are unchanged.
   Remove the ld_s / ld_hx / ld_wx EX/MEM fields once unused.

2. Divider prep cycle (cone 5). At start, latch the RAW post-forward
   operands (quo_q <= a, dvs_q <= b) and the sign flags (a_neg, b_neg,
   q_neg as today; q_neg's b != 0 term can be formed from dvs_q in the
   prep cycle if it shows up on a path). Add one prep cycle in the real
   (non-ALTOPS) branch: quo_q <= a_neg_q ? -quo_q : quo_q,
   dvs_q <= b_neg_q ? -dvs_q : dvs_q, rem_q <= 0, then the existing 32
   iterations. This takes both negate carry chains off the EX forward
   mux -> divider-flop path (they now start at divider flops). The
   ALTOPS branch is untouched (still done one cycle after start, so
   liveness/formal timing is unchanged). Cost: +1 cycle per DIV/REM.

3. Dedicated B/J/U immediate for the ID pc + imm adder (cone 8).
   pc_imm (-> ID/EX.br_target) only matters for BRANCH, JAL and AUIPC
   (take target, JAL jtgt, AUIPC early group, RVFI redirect_target).
   Feed the adder from imm_bju = instr[2] ? (instr[3] ? J-imm : U-imm)
   : B-imm. That is one LUT per bit on raw word bits (instr[2], instr[3]
   and up to 3 candidate bits), instead of imm_gen's 7-bit opcode case
   (2 levels). imm_gen keeps feeding everything else (ID/EX.imm, b_val,
   br_misalign, jal_misalign, tr_en, ...), so semantics are unchanged.
   For any non-B/J/U instruction br_target is a don't-care (never
   selected: alu_auipc / take / !jlink jump are all 0 for it).

None of the three adds a consumer to DO, the DSP outputs, br_lt_v/take,
dmem_ready/stall or the PC mux, and none adds a pipeline-register copy
of a control net. The expected outcome is that the logged worst cone and two
other wall cones lose about 0.3-0.6 ns each. The remaining wall cones (EX
forward -> compare -> take -> kill/PC, shifter -> oth_q, imem -> 32:1
regfile read, dmem_ready -> PC, DSP -> ID bypass) cap the median gain,
so the expected gain is small: about +2-5%, mostly from option 0 and from
whichever of these three cones limits options 1/2.

Implementer checklist: (a) before editing, run `make timing TARGET=bench`
on the champion and record the top paths of ALL three placement options
(not only option 0), so this round can be compared per-option (r8s0);
(b) after editing, confirm with the same command that the three cones
lost their levels and that no new path appears in their place, and record
the per-option Fmax and top-path list in implementation_notes; (c) run
cosim --istall --dstall: cycles must be 4,251,815 + (number of timed
DIV/REM), i.e. effectively unchanged; (d) test_alu.py and the divider
vectors must pass (real arithmetic), and `make formal` (ALTOPS) must pass
unchanged.

Update any latency expectation to start + prep + 32 iterations + done (real branch only); keep all result vectors passing and add sign corners (INT_MIN/-1, x/0, neg/neg, neg/pos for DIV and REM). test_alu.py / test_pipeline.py must pass unchanged (LB/LH sign-fill loads covered by cosim).

lesson: - 2026-10-01 hyp-20261001-001-r14s0 (regression, -4.76%): Three zero-CPI cuts that each took a LUT level or a carry chain off one wall cone of the champion (pre-ANDed per-lane sign-fill flops sf_h/sf_w with syn_keep'd X/Y fill nets, a divider prep cycle that negates quo_q/dvs_q in place, and a B/J/U-only imm_bju mux feeding the ID pc+imm adder) scored 282.69, which at the ~unchanged 4,251,815 cycles means a ~120.2 MHz median against r11s1's 126.2, so at least one of the two 126.2 MHz placement options lost ~6 MHz (the per-option split and path lists required by checklist items (a)/(b) were not logged, so the culprit is unknown); unlike r10s1/r11s1, which deleted logic outright (a whole stage, ~100 flops, a mux leg), every cut here shortened its cone by adding logic next to the old logic (imm_bju is a second immediate mux beside the kept imm_gen, so raw imem word bits, including the rs1/rs2 address bits that drive the 32:1 regfile read, gain loads, and instr[2]/instr[3] drive dozens of new LUTs; D7/D15/D23/D31 each drive two fill LUTs; the divider flops gain an extra D-mux source and three new flops), and r8s0's losing bundle (-4.93%) also contained the divider prep cycle, so judge "subtractive" by the net cells and loads on wall nets rather than by the levels in one cone, and try such cuts one per slot with all three placement options timed, because a bundle hides which cut paid and which cost.

title: Stall-cover I-cache: an ahead-read 2K-entry BSRAM instruction cache whose registered output feeds ID only when io_imemReady = 0, hiding most of the ~0.77M imem-stall bubbles
motivation:
The imem bus stall is now by far the biggest cycle cost on the r11s1
champion (4,251,815 cycles, 126.2 MHz). r13s2's cosim (--istall --dstall)
counted ~195K imem stalls it could hide by banking words during backend
holds plus 578,140 imem bubbles that still arrived with the queue empty,
so roughly 0.77M cycles (~18%) go to io_imemReady = 0. The other sources
are much smaller: load-use ~208K, MUL-use ~36K, all control flow ~69K
(r12s2/r13s0). r13s2 concluded that hiding imem stalls behind backend holds
tops out near 6% and that "a further attack on imem stalls needs fetch
bandwidth above 1 word/cycle (or fewer stalls)". A core-internal
instruction store gives exactly that: on a hit, the word does not need the
bus at all. ARCHITECTURE.md explicitly allows caches ("logic that handles
or hides stalls is part of the timed circuit"), and log.jsonl has no cache
attempt so far.
Every fetch-buffer idea lost Fmax by putting the stall net or a mux at the
fetch/ID boundary (r6s1 -4.0%, r8s1 -1.9%, r13s1 -7.3%). Each of them was
chasing only a 4-6% cycle cut, though. This one targets ~14%. That leaves
room to pay r6s1's measured price of one LUT level on the ID word
(~0.4-0.5 ns) and still clear the 4.6% bar.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add an L1 instruction cache (new rtl/icache.sv) that never sits on the
normal fetch path. It only stands in for the bus on cycles where
io_imemReady = 0. The core keeps its exact fetch/redirect structure (PC
flop -> io_imemAddr, IF/ID word combinational, fetch_pred's inc_q in the
PC loop). The only datapath change on the ID front end is one 2:1 select
whose select is a flop:
    ID word  = imem_ready ? io_imemData : cq_word
    ID valid = imem_ready | use_c
with use_c = cq_hit & (cq_addr == pc). This is a flop-vs-flop equality and
never uses take, br_lt_v or the AGU.

Organization: direct-mapped, 2048 x {valid, tag[31:13], word[31:0]} in
inferred BSRAM (zero-initialised with an `initial` loop like fetch_pred,
so valid = 0 at reset), ~7 of the 46 GW2A BSRAMs. If timing or BSRAM
cascading hurts, fall back to 1024 entries (4 KB).

Ahead read: BSRAM DO is late (~2 ns after other registers, r3s0), so it
must never feed ID directly. The cache is read one cycle early and its
output is registered:
  - Address register (absorbed into the BSRAM ADB): ca_d = predicted PC of
    the NEXT-NEXT fetch, built only from registered or early terms in
    parallel with pc_alt:
        ca_d = hold ? pc4 : (jump ? jtgt4 : pc + inc1_q)
    pc4 is IF's existing carry-chain pc + 4. inc1_q = inc_q + 1 is a new
    fetch_pred flop beside inc_q (computed from the same table read, or
    stored pre-incremented by the MEM-side trainer, so that no adder sits
    after the DO). jtgt4 = jlink ? link4 : br_target4, with link4 = pc + 8
    and br_target4 = pc + imm + 4 as two new ID/EX flops computed in ID
    next to link / br_target. Nothing take-, JALR-AGU- or compare-derived
    enters ca_d (r6s2/r10s2 rules). A fabric copy ca_q of the full address
    is kept beside it.
  - Output register (one cycle later): cq_word <= DO.word;
    cq_hit <= DO.valid && DO.tag == ca_q[31:13]; cq_addr <= ca_q[31:2].
    This is a short DO -> tag compare -> flop path with no wide sink.
When the guess was wrong (a taken branch / JALR redirect, a
fetch_pred-predicted taken B/J, a hold the guess did not see), cq_addr !=
pc and the cache simply does not cover that cycle. That is always safe.

Fill: every successful bus fetch (imem_ready, the PC) is latched into a
registered write port {we_q, waddr_q, wtag_q, wdata_q} and written one
cycle later. The write uses flops only, the same discipline as r11s1's
w_q regfile port. Coherence is not needed. test/cosim/main.cpp keeps
separate imem[] and dmem[] arrays (both loaded from the ELF), so stores
never change instruction memory. formal/checks_si.cfg has no imem
consistency check (insn/reg/pc_fwd/pc_bwd/causal/unique/cover/ill/liveness
only), and a cached word is a word the bus delivered earlier for that same
full PC. FENCE.I stays a NOP as now. The full 30-bit cq_addr == pc compare
plus the full tag [31:13] keep the lookup exact for any symbolic PC.

Hazard wiring: hazard_unit gets imem_stall = !imem_ready && !use_c (use_c
computed in parallel with the load-use compare). flush_if uses the same
term. The PC and fetch_pred advance exactly as on an imem_ready cycle.

Cosim gate (mandatory before synthesis; --istall --dstall reproduces the
FPGA stall pattern cycle for cycle): log cycles, imem-stall cycles,
stalls covered by the cache, cold misses and wrong-guess cycles. Build
only if cycles <= 3.85M (-9.5%). Expected: ~0.55-0.65M covered ->
~3.6-3.7M cycles (-13 to -15%). Then record the cycles/Fmax split and the
top timing paths for all three placement options in implementation_notes.

Expected Fmax cost: one LUT on the ID word (r6s1: ~0.4-0.5 ns) plus
possibly one level on the imem_stall -> hold term, so ~126 -> ~116-120
MHz. Net: 0.93-0.95 x 1.15-1.17, about +7-11%.

title: Next-fetch word predictor: 64-entry ahead-read L0 word table supplies the ID instruction on imem-stall cycles
motivation:
Branch/jump bubbles total only ~69K cycles (~1.6% of r11s1's 4,251,815), so
no direction or target predictor can clear the 4.6% bar (r13s0). The core is
fetch-bound: 2.92M instructions retire in the timed window (measured with
test/cosim/reference.py between the 0x10000100/0x10000104 markers), and the
imem port delivers <= 0.781 words/cycle, so ~0.8M cycles are imem-stall
bubbles. r13s2 showed that banking words behind backend holds can hide at
most ~6% because a 1-word/cycle front end cannot run ahead; its lesson asks
for "fewer stalls". A fetch cycle needs no imem response at all if the word
at the next fetch PC can be predicted from a small table of previously
fetched words. Measured on the same 2.92M-PC trace, a direct-mapped
tagged word table (1 word/entry, filled on every delivered fetch) hits
64.0% (32 entries), 71.5% (64), 83.3% (128), 93.8% (256); the hot static
footprint is 1,670 words. (A loop-buffer variant keyed on backward-taken
edges reached only 30% at 8 entries and 51% at 16, so the plain tagged
table is the better predictor.)

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add rtl/fetch_word.sv, a 64-entry (keep the size a parameter; try 128 if
64 is Fmax-neutral) word table {v, tag = pc[19:8], word[31:0]} in LUT-RAM,
read one cycle AHEAD so that everything ID sees from it is a flop:
  - Read index = pcn[7:2], where pcn = pc[31:2] + inc on its own
    syn_keep'd carry chain (a duplicate of if_stage's pc_inc; do NOT load
    the existing pc_inc / pc_reg / pc_alt nets, which sit on the PC -> PC
    wall cone). pcn is the next fetch PC whenever the PC neither holds nor
    is redirected.
  - Registered: lbw_q <= word, lb_use_q <= v && tag == pcn[19:8] && !blk,
    where blk = ID/EX.br_ok | ID/EX.ctrl.is_jump (registered kill bits:
    any branch, JALR, unpredicted JAL or p_bad in EX may redirect the PC
    away from pcn) | reset. On hold, lbw_q holds and lb_use_q <=
    lb_use_q && !blk (the PC holds too, so the held word is still the
    word at PC). take, br_lt_v, jalr_go and agu_sum get NO new consumer
    (r8s2/r10s2/r11s2 rule); the block term only costs coverage after a
    branch, which the trace model puts at ~20% of hits.
  - ID word = lb_use_q ? lbw_q : io_imemData (a LUT3 per bit on flops; use
    2-4 syn_preserve copies of lb_use_q so no copy drives >16 loads).
    IF/ID.valid = imem_ready | lb_use_q; hazard_unit's imem_stall becomes
    !imem_ready && !lb_use_q (both flops, should fold into the existing
    stall_if LUT tree).
  - Fill: synchronous write at pc[7:2] of {1, pc[19:8], io_imemData} when
    imem_ready (PC and imem data are flops, so the write port adds no
    combinational depth). Wrong-path fetches still write correct words.
  - Coherence: a 64-bit flop valid vector; a store in MEM (EX/MEM.mem_write
    && !stall, registered one cycle) clears v[mem_addr[7:2]], and a FENCE /
    FENCE.I in ID clears all. CoreMark never writes code; formal ties
    imemReady=1 and has no imem-consistency check, so lb_use_q only has to
    be a correct word for the PC in cosim. Liveness is unaffected (the
    table can only remove stall cycles).
Correctness argument: when !blk and !hold in cycle c-1, PC(c) = pc_reg =
pc + inc_q = pcn (the jump term is in blk, take and jalr_go need
br_ok / is_jump in ID/EX), and the tag compare covers pc[19:8] (all PCs are
inside the 1 MiB window; compare the full pc[31:8] if area allows), so
lbw_q is exactly the word at PC(c).
Expected cycles: hits on ~57% of fetches after the block loss, times
~0.8M imem-stall bubbles, times ~0.75 not already hidden behind backend
holds (r13s2's 195K / 773K) gives ~340K cycles, i.e. 4.25M -> ~3.9M (-8%).
Fmax cost: one LUT3 level on the imem -> 32:1 regfile read -> ID/EX wall
cone (r6s1: ~0.4-0.5 ns; at 7.92 ns ~5%) plus a new duplicate carry chain
and LUT-RAM area. Net +3..+8%.
GATE (mandatory, before synthesis): run cosim with --istall --dstall and
report cycles, lb_use count and table hit rate. Ship only if cycles <=
3.95M (-7%); if 64 entries miss the gate, try 128 (83% hit) before giving up.
Log the cycles/Fmax split and the top timing paths of all three placement
options.

lesson: - 2026-10-01 hyp-20261001-003-r14s2 (regression, -22.57%): A 64-entry ahead-read word table (fetch_word.sv: a table indexed by a duplicate pcn = pc + inc carry chain with a 12-bit tag compare, registered lbw_q/lb_use_q, ID word = per-byte `lb_use ? lbw_q : io_imemData`, imem_stall = !imem_ready && !lb_use) followed r14s1's rule that an imem-stall cover must reach ID only as precomputed flops, yet scored 229.85; since fitness = Fmax*1e7/cycles and the table can only remove stall cycles, that is <= ~97.7 MHz even at the unchanged 4,251,815 cycles (~90.8 MHz at its 3.95M gate) against r11s1's 126.2, a >= 2.3 ns loss, ~5x the one-LUT3 price on the ID word (the cosim counters, split and paths were not logged); the likely cause is that "compare a cycle early" does not remove the lookup, it moves it into a new flop-to-flop path (PC flop -> pcn carry chain -> 64-deep table read -> tag compare -> blk/hold mux -> lb_use_q) that by itself can exceed 7.92 ns, while the late pc_hold stall net also picked up the lbw_q CE / lb_use_q D-mux loads (cf. r10s0) and a fence decode on the muxed ID word now drives the 64 valid flops; so registering the use flag is necessary but not sufficient: before cosim, time the table's own index -> read -> compare -> flop chain against the champion's period (split it over two cycles if it does not fit) and keep hold off the table's flops, and note that r6s1, r8s1, r13s1, r14s1 and r14s2 have now all lost (-1.9% to -22.6%) with a core-side word source at the fetch/ID boundary.

title: Single cut on the champion's worst cone: sign fill from two shared half-sign nets, no fill LUT level after dmem DO
motivation:
r11s1's logged worst path (126.2 MHz on placement options 1/2, 115.3 on
option 0) is dmem DO -> u_mem load align -> u_id reg_q.rs2_val_12, 5 cells,
and r14s0's worst path was the same cone (DO -> b_val_31). Bits [31:8]
of the bypassed load data go DO -> ld_sign (8-input 4:1 AND-OR of
DO[7/15/23/31] on ld_s, 2 LUT levels) -> fill LUT ((ld_w & DO) |
(ld_wx & ld_sign), or the h0/h2/hx 3-term mix for [15:8]) -> the ID merge
LUT -> ID/EX flop: 4 LUT levels after the latest-arriving signal in the
design, while the byte lanes [7:0] need only 3. ld_wx is logically
redundant (ld_s is already 0 for word and unsigned loads), and ld_hx only
differs from ld_s by excluding halfword loads, so the extra fill level is
a product of how the sign is shared, not of the function. r14s0 bundled a
related cut with two others (imm_bju mux, divider prep cycle, which r8s0
also lost with) and lost -4.76% without logging which cut cost, so the
sign cut itself was never measured alone.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Make the load-sign cut alone, strictly subtractive in levels and with no
